source.title: DILA: Dictionary Label Attention for Mechanistic Interpretability in High-dimensional Multi-label Medical Coding Prediction
source.authors: John Wu; David Wu; Ji-Meng Sun

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether dictionary learning can recover interpretable sparse features in a medical language-model setting, which is a new application setting for the LLM feature-recovery claim.
record.gate_note: The paper measures identification and human evaluation of sparse dictionary features versus dense activations and random contexts. It does not measure toy-network geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, feature importance versus capacity allocation, or feature dimensionality. The weight-ablation, code-prediction, and coding-performance experiments assess the DILA mechanism or task performance rather than those claim versions, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains a sparse autoencoder on medical RoBERTa token embeddings for ICD coding. It uses blinded expert and LLM identification tests to compare dictionary features against dense label-attention neurons and random contexts. These results bear on V4, the claim that a dictionary recovers interpretable sparse features in a real language model, in a new domain. Most of the paper (ablation, predictability, coding performance) concerns its own DILA method. The SAE is also trained jointly with the task loss, so this is not a purely post-hoc recovery.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors claim sparse dictionary embeddings are at least 50% more human-understandable than dense counterparts. They say over 3,000 interpretable concepts were 'hidden in superposition'. They hold that medical LLMs, while imperfect, can scale feature identification, and that DILA keeps competitive coding performance. They acknowledge unidentifiable features and LLM summary errors.
record.recipe_differences: Applies a sparse autoencoder and dictionary label-attention module to medical coding embeddings and evaluates feature interpretability; it does not reproduce the original toy-model setup or its geometry and sparsity sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM–human alignment on feature identification (cosine 0.77, Jaccard 0.62) is higher for dictionary features than for dense Z (0.59/0.43) or random (0.15/0.08).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated LLM interpretation agrees better with experts on SAE features than on dense neurons.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to a medical coding model and task. Human evaluations use two experts and samples of 100 features. The paper reports unidentifiable features and imperfect LLM summaries; it does not directly measure feature geometry, representation completeness, stability, or capacity allocation.
record.rows_left_out: None of the eligible feature-identification and summary-evaluation rows were omitted. Results in Tables 4-7 and the code-mapping predictability experiments were left out because they evaluate DILA's prediction effects, debugging, or feature-to-code mappings rather than feature recovery or the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transitions.
All of it: no importance or capacity allocation analysis.

Whether features are spread across many neurons in the same layer. The dense Z comparator is a different (tanh-projected label-attention) layer, not the SAE's input embedding neurons. Generality beyond one medical RoBERTa model is also untested.
Completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, and canonicality of SAE features. Reconstruction quality is not reported.

missing.what: Only 5,847 of 6,088 active features had at least 4 activating contexts; features with fewer were deemed unidentifiable before testing.
missing.locator: Appendix A.3, 'Other Minor Identification Experiment Details'

missing.what: The SAE dictionary size m, reconstruction error and the number of dead features are not reported. The SAE is fine-tuned jointly with the BCE task loss (Eq. 8), not trained purely post hoc.

record.verdict_notes: Interpretability evidence for V4 rests on two expert raters and 100-feature samples, with no significance tests. The dense comparator is a different layer (tanh label-attention projection) from the SAE input, so the sparse-versus-dense comparison is not within the same representation. Summary-agreement samples were 59 (dictionary f) and 34 (dense Z), per A.4.2.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

The study tests dictionary recovery of sparse features in a medical coding model; it does not test the separate claim that features are spread across many neurons, nor does it establish generality across LLMs, model families, or tasks.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

relationships.condition: SAE (dictionary f) on medical RoBERTa embeddings for MIMIC-III ICD coding, versus dense label-attention Z and random contexts
relationships.reason: Dictionary features are identified at 0.67/0.69 by experts and 0.58–0.59 by the LLM. This compares with 0.34–0.43 for dense Z and 0.19–0.27 for random (r1–r4). 3,524 features were LLM-identified versus 263 (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Experts identified dictionary features at 0.67/0.69 and the LLM at 0.58–0.59, against 0.34–0.43 for dense label attention and 0.19–0.27 for random contexts. The LLM identified 3,524 features versus 263.

tranche.reason: Tests dictionary-feature interpretability in the new setting of medical RoBERTa embeddings and high-dimensional ICD coding, using expert and LLM identification controls.

source_check.notes: LLM identification failure does not establish that an underlying concept is absent or irrecoverable. These results provide indirect interpretability evidence, without testing superposition geometry or canonical SAE units.

statements.correction: Table 1: expert dictionary accuracies 0.67 and 0.69; dense Z accuracies 0.43 and 0.42. Section 3.2: SAE pretraining followed by joint end-to-end training. Dense Z: PLM-ICD label-attention activations. Code availability stated. Supplied text: preprint under review.
statements.problem: The medical results, training description, comparator distinction, controls and code availability match. Reviewed status is not established by the supplied text, which is marked preprint under review.

reader_labels.reason: Human and LLM identification evaluations, and human agreement with summaries, support recovery of interpretable sparse features in this setting (r1-r3, r5-r6, r22-r25).
